## Part A – Creating Data Frames
**Question #1:**

a. Create a vector
```{r}
scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
```


b. Sort the scores in ascending order and descending order. What is the output?
```{r}
sort(scores)
sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)
```


c. Print your sorted result from sort-ascending. Check whether the # names (“Ana”, “Ben”, …) stayed attached to their correct values.
```{r}
sort_ascending <- sort(scores)
sort_ascending
```


d. Create another vectors
```{r}
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE") 
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)
```


e. Sort subjects alphabetically using sort()
```{r}
sort(subjects)
```


f. Sort incomplete using sort(). Observe what happens to the NA
```{r}
# values by default.
sort(incomplete)
# TODO: Now sort it again using na.last = TRUE so the NAs appear at the end
sort(incomplete, na.last = TRUE)
```

**Question #2:**

- When you sorted scores, did the names stay correctly attached to their original values?
- Explain why this matters: if you were sorting exam scores to find the top performer, what would go wrong if the names did NOT follow their values?

**Answer:** The names stay correctly attached to their original values when sorted. Thsi matters when sorting exam scores and determining the top performer because if the names did not follow their values the result would be inaccurate and the top performer title might be given to someone else instead of the right one.


**Question #3:**

- By default, sort() silently removes NA values instead of showing them or throwing an error.
- Why might this default behavior be dangerous if you were reporting “the lowest score” in a dataset with missing data, without first checking for NA values?.

**Answer:** The default behavior might be dangerous when reporting lowest score because R removes the NA values instead of throwing error or warning which might result to innacurate result or inaccurate minimum values. 


**Question #4:**

Use order(scores) and print the result. Compare this output to the sort(scores) output. What is the difference?
```{r}
order(scores)
sort(scores)
```

**Answer:** The sort(scores) returns the actual value while order(scores) returns the index positions of the values to arrange them into ascending order.

Use the result of order(scores) to index scores itself: # Compare this to sort(scores) – they should produce the same values.
- Do they have the same values? Explain briefly.
```{r}
scores[order(scores)]
```

**Answer:** Yes, because indexing _scores_ in order, by using the ordered position it arranges the values in ascending order which is the same as the result when sorting the _scores_.


**Question #5:**

Create a dataframe from these vectors name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio") score = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74) section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
- What is the output?
```{r}
students <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio"),
  score = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74),
  section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
)
students
```


- Reorder the ENTIRE students data frame by score using students[order(students$score), ]
What is the output?
```{r}
students [order(students$score), ]
```


- Reorder students by score in DESCENDING order.
```{r}
students [order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```


**Question #6:**

sort(scores) and scores[order(scores)] produce the same final values, but they work completely differently under the hood.
- In your own words, explain what order(scores) actually returns (look at the raw numbers it gives you), and why that output is useless on its own unless you use it to index something.

**Answer:** _order(scores)_ returns the positional infeces of the values in their sorted arrangements. These indeces are numbers that remains useless and meaningless unless they are used to rearrange vectors, matrix, and even data frames because it will return the values in now sorted order.


**Question #7:**

Explain why sort() alone could NOT have been used to reorder the whole students data frame by score (try to imagine running sort(students) and think about what “sorting a table” would even mean).
- Why is order() the correct tool whenever you need to keep multiple related columns lined up with each other?

**Answer:** sort() only works on a single vector and returns values in ascending or descending order. It can't be used to reorder the whole students data frame by scores because it will only sort the score column, leaving the names and section on the same spot which can distort the data and misleading information. order() is the correct tool when dealing with multiple columns because it maintains its relationship with the rows when sorting a specific column like the _scores_. It needs the index position of the value when sorted, and from there, sorting a specific column also matches or attached its value on the same row in another column.


**Question #8:**
```{r} 
# TODO: Use rank(scores) and print the result. 
# Print scores, then rank(scores), side by side (e.g., using 
#cbind(scores, rank(scores))) so you can see which score got which rank
rank(scores)
cbind(scores, rank(scores))
```

- a. Ranking the output for Ben and Dex
```{r}
# TODO: Look at the rank() output for Ben and Dex.
rank(scores)[c("Ben", "Dex")]
```

- What rank did each of them receive?

**Answer:** Both received 6.5 rank

- Ben and Dex both scored 92, the highest score in the class, but under the default rank() they did NOT both simply get rank “1” or rank “7” as a whole number. Explain exactly what value they received by default and why R computes it that way for tied values.

**Answer:** Both of them received 6.5 because rank() uses ties.method when there are the same values. By default, ties.method gets the average of 6 and 7 position and the calculated value will be assigned to the ones who tied instead of returning whole number.


**Question #8:**

a. Create a data frame.
sales <- data.frame( employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"), units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)

- Add a column sales$rank that ranks employees by units_sold, with the TOP seller receiving rank 1.

```{r}
sales <- data.frame(
  employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)
sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)
sales
```


b. Reorder the entire sales data frame using order() so it is displayed from HIGHEST units_sold to LOWEST.
```{r}
sales_ordered <- sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]
sales_ordered
```


**Question #9:**

- In this challenge, you used rank() to determine standing and order() to determine display order.
- Could you have used order() alone to solve the entire problem (both awarding ranks AND reordering the table)?
- Explain what order() is missing that rank() provides, using your own words rather than repeating the definitions

**Answer:** order() alone cannot solve the problem especially that there's an awarding based on ranks. order() simply determines the sequential positions of values and does not do some calculations like dtermining the relative position of one from another. While as for rank() it measures the relative standings to every values and also handles ties, in which order() sorts the ranks after.
